## **Abstract**

Recent studies indicate that migration is the period of highest mortality for neotropical migrant birds.  The increasing scarcity, particularly in the northeastern U. S., of suitable places to rest, feed, and escape predation during migration contributes to this mortality.  In the Great Lakes region, the importance of “stopover sites” is heightened by the lakes themselves, which are large areas completely unsuitable for migrating land birds to land, but that provide important spring food sources in the form of emergent aquatic insects.  Conservation of migratory birds, including many “species of greatest conservation need,” requires protecting a network of stopover sites, particularly in the highly‐altered Lake Ontario watershed.  Using data collected by skilled volunteers across multiple years during both spring and fall, we developed predictive GIS models of stopover habitat for the southern portion of Lake Ontario’s watershed in NY based on the species richness and abundance of migrants. Our on‐the‐ground data for this region confirm that predictions based on radar and studies in other parts of the Great Lakes are valid for our region as well, and that they hold up surprisingly well for fall migration as well as spring migration.  Both species richness and abundance of migrants is greater closer to the shores of Lake Ontario than farther inland.  This pattern holds in the fall as well as the spring, but the band of higher concentration of migrants is wider in the fall, extending out to approximately 8 km.  Woody habitat within diverse inland wetland complexes, such as those around Montezuma and Iroquois‐Tonawanda‐Oak Orchard Wetland Complexes, may also harbor high concentrations of migrants within our study area.  Migrants are also concentrated within suitable habitat that is surrounded and isolated by matrices of developed and agricultural cover.  Indeed, contrary to some studies in other areas, the percentage of urban cover and road density within the landscape are better predictors than the percentage of cover of suitable habitat.  These relationships suggest migrants are squeezing into patches of suitable cover in landscapes where such cover is limited by other predominant land uses.  Overall, these models using only landscape‐scale predictors explain between 8 and 35% of the variation in migrant distributions, while the full models including fine‐scale habitat predictors explained between 31 and 41% of the variation.  Consequently, we are confident that these maps, in combination with assessments of habitat quality based on important vegetation structural elements, as recommended by the accompanying user guide, can help guide and focus stopover habitat conservation and management efforts within the study area.

## **Executive Summary/Quick Guide**

This is the complete technical report detailing the results of a three‐year study of migratory birds in central and western New York near Lake Ontario.  For this study, 55 expert birders surveyed more than 50 randomly selected patches of woody habitat for migratory land birds in both spring and fall.  These sites, which were surveyed numerous times each season, were located in suitable woody habitat within a variety of landscapes, from the shoreline of the lake to nearly 40 miles inland, within largely forested areas as well as in urban and agricultural areas.  The results of the surveys allowed us to determine what kinds of sites in what kinds of areas tend to have more migrant birds (higher abundance) as well as more kinds of migrant birds (higher species richness).  Using these on‐the‐ground data, we developed models to predict what places within this region of New York support greater abundance and species richness of migratory land birds.

## _**Location matters**_

In both spring and fall, migrant richness and abundance are predicted to be greatest within a few kilometers of Lake Ontario, with the zone of high use extending farther inland in the fall.  Isolated patches of woody cover within urban and suburban matrices near Lakes Ontario and Erie also are predicted to support higher abundance and richness of migrants in spring and fall, as are areas of natural cover within and around Iroquois‐Tonawanda‐ Oak Orchard and Montezuma Wetland Complexes.  Finally, in both spring and fall, migrant richness and abundance are predicted to be higher in patches of stopover habitat surrounded by a variety of different natural land cover types.

## _**Habitat matters too**_

Although the models used to create the map, which of course can only use landscape scale variables that we can translate into a GIS framework, explain a considerable amount of the variation in migrant distributions (20‐35%, but only 8% for fall richness), habitat structure and composition on the ground also matter particularly in the fall.  Migrant abundance and richness were higher at locations with more than 40% shrub cover in the understory less than 2 m above the ground in both seasons, but particularly in the fall.  The density of stems and the number of fruiting species were also important predictors in the fall.

## _**But migrants are using almost the entire landscape**_

It is important to point out that migrating land birds can be found in a wide variety of habitats, from large patches of mature forest to ornamental shrubs and trees in residential areas.  Because they are spread out across the airspace as they fly overhead at night, they will land in many different kinds of places at dawn. While data presented here show that they are not distributed uniformly across the landscape when stopping over, the “hotspots,” or areas of concentrated abundance and/or richness, are not orders of magnitude more “hot” than the rest of the landscape.  The “hotspots” may be areas to focus conservation action, particularly in areas where there is little other potential suitable habitat for migrants, but effective conservation of migratory land birds will require a diffuse network of stopover sites, and efforts to improve habitat for migrants by ensuring good shrub cover and diverse food resources is likely valuable _anywhere on the map_ .

## _**Suggestions for how to interpret and use maps included in this report**_

The resulting maps included in this report, a few of which are also included in an accompanying guide for interested landowners, show stopover habitat predicted to have relatively more migrant birds and/or more species of migrant birds during spring and/or fall seasons.  There are two composite maps of predicted “hotspots” map showing only the sites predicted to have especially high numbers and species of migrants.  The first shows all of these hotspots, with the darker colors representing sites that are predicted to have either high

abundance and richness or to have high values in both spring and fall.  The second hotspot map should be used to aid in interpretation of the first map‐‐‐it shows which sites are predicted to be important in both seasons as opposed to having extremely high abundance or richness in only spring or fall.  Both of these “hotspot” maps show that migrants are concentrated near Lake Ontario, in isolated patches near urban areas and to a lesser extent in agricultural areas, and inland around the Finger Lakes and Iroquois‐Tonawanda‐Oak Orchard and Montezuma Wetlands Complexes.

Importantly, these “hotspot” maps are only suggestions of places that conservation action might be focused. They only “capture” approximately 22% of the spring migrants using the study region, and only 7% of the fall migrants.  Migrants are likely using nearly all woody habitat within our study area to some extent.  We encourage all users to consider the maps showing the predictions for abundance and richness for spring and fall separately, as they show more than just the sites predicted to have the highest values—only the lowest values are de‐emphasized on this map.  Note that the range on these maps is not huge—the higher abundance and richness sites are not orders of magnitude higher than the lowest part of the range.  Our models do under predict the “hotspots” among our own sampling sites, but the full range between the “best” sites and “worst” sites for among our sampling sites was 0.25‐ 9.14 average number of spring migrants per day and 0‐27 average number of fall migrants per day.

When using our maps to identify potential stopover habitat, users should keep in mind the following:

1) These maps only take into account landscape variables that we could incorporate into a GIS framework, because the fine detail about habitat composition and structure that we collected at our study sites, and which is also important, is not available for the entire study area.

2) As with any remotely sensed land cover dataset, there are errors in the base land cover data that we used.

3) These maps only show pixels that are classed as some kind of woody cover in a remotely sensed land cover dataset, and furthermore eliminate tiny clusters of potentially suitable habitat.  Migrating land birds may use backyards, street tree canopies, and other tiny patches of habitat as well.  However, our minimum patch size may be smaller than the feasible scales for most conservation action, and patches smaller than that may not be ideal for migrant fitness.

4) These maps are applicable to land birds only.  Since we limited our sampling to wooded areas, our results are not applicable to grassland birds, wetland birds, shorebirds or waterfowl, and they are likely not applicable to raptors either, since those species migrate during the day and use thermals to travel along and around the lakeshore.

With those cautions, we think these maps, as well as the information we gained about the importance of shrub cover and other habitat features, can be used to help prioritize areas for stopover habitat conservation and management.  Migrants are definitely concentrated along the shoreline in both spring and fall, and this “band” of migrants extends farther back from the shoreline than perhaps previously thought, particularly in the fall. Areas with high or moderate values that are fairly isolated from other potential habitat may also be particularly important, provided the habitat offers protection and food resources.

## **Introduction**

The Great Lakes, particularly coastal and nearshore areas, provide globally or continentally important stopover sites (http://iba.audubon.org/iba/prioritySiteIndex.do?priority=Global;

http://www.ibacanada/explore.jsp?lang=en) for all groups of migratory land‐ and waterbirds.  Hundreds of millions of migrating birds cross the Great Lakes region each spring and fall, and they encounter a highly altered landscape with limited opportunities to rest, feed, and escape predation during this risky period‐‐up to 85% of annual mortality of adult birds can occur during these mass movements (Moore 2000, Sillette & Holmes 2002). The need for stopover sites to rest and feed is particularly critical for birds near the Great Lakes, where many of the 100+ species pause to wait for favorable weather conditions to cross the lakes at night.  Other species lengthen their flights by traveling around the perimeter of the lakes (Agard and Spellman 2004, Ewert _et al_ . 2006). Further, food availability may be greater in riparian, wetland, and near‐shore habitats where flying insects that reproduce in water may be more abundant (Smith et al. 2007).  Much of the Great Lakes’ coastal aquatic and terrestrial landscapes that once supported migrating birds have been lost or degraded, and remaining habitat continues to be threatened by several trends, including development, habitat conversion, water quality degradation, invasive species, recreational and consumptive activities, towers, climate change and associated responses to climate change, such as alternative energy development (Chipley 2003, Ontario Important Bird Area Project, Soulliere et al. 2007a).  Managers urgently need a tool for identifying the distinguishing attributes of critical migratory stopover sites so that these areas may be located and conserved, particularly in highly altered and changing landscapes like the Great Lakes region (Faaborg et al. 2010, Great Lakes Wind Collaborative 2011).

Land birds are particularly challenged to find suitable stopover habitat in the Great Lakes region.  Agricultural and urban land uses have transformed much of the region’s woody habitat into inhospitable areas, and the lakes themselves are large expanses of inhospitable habitat.  For at least some songbird species, migration is the period of the life cycle when adult birds suffer the highest mortality (Sillett and Holmes 2002).  Land birds typically use several stopover sites en route between wintering and breeding areas (Moore 2000); these sites provide locations for migrants to refuel and seek shelter from weather and predators (Petit 2000).  During the spring, migrants build the reserves needed for reproduction at stopover sites (Petrie and Wilcox 2003, Badzinski and Petrie 2006). But not all stopover sites, or the landscapes in which they occur, are of equal value to migrants (Petit 2000, Mehlman et al. 2005).  The relative importance of stopover sites to overall fitness likely varies by species, and may also be subject to carry‐over effects between wintering and breeding grounds (e.g., Runge and Marra 2005).  In a review, Newton (2006) concluded that “any factors that increase the cost of migration, especially in spring, could influence subsequent population size.”

Although awareness of the importance of stopover habitat for bird conservation has grown in recent years, conservation frameworks are still in the early stages of development.  Where do we need to protect habitat, and how much?  For land birds in particular, migration seems to be a diffuse phenomenon, with migrants moving as a front, or in waves, with wide variability from year to year.  There is little evidence of stopover site fidelity (but see Vogt et al. 2012), and there are not yet clear known migration “corridors” as there are for waterfowl and raptors.  From a conservation standpoint, sites that offer a variety of food resources may be important, because they can provide fuel to a variety of species, have a greater chance of offering food every year, and may buffer against the negative consequences of phenological mismatches that may occur with climate change (Hall and Root 2012) during the relatively short spring migration.  But land birds are able to use small sites with varying degrees of naturalness, successfully accumulating body reserves during migration at highly landscaped urban parks (Mehlman et al. 2005, Seewagen and Slayton 2008).  Consequently, the general consensus is that, for land birds, “the provision of good habitats well distributed across the landscape in preferred migration pathways seems like a safe strategy to protect en route migrants, with the addition of sites in areas where larger barriers

to migration may exist, such as along the Gulf of Mexico or Great Lakes.”   In these places, “any little fragment of forest, field, or wetland may be valuable on occasion” (Faaborg et al. 2010, Mehlman et al. 2005).  While this is probably correct, as a course of conservation action, it is difficult to execute.  Conservation funding, time, and other resources are limited, making efficiency and prioritization necessary.  Also, because several migratory species are in decline, conservation actions should have the greatest impact possible.  Thus, there is considerable interest in prioritizing where to implement conservation practices among the array of stopover sites to maximize benefits of conservation efforts to migrants.

To provide this focus and inform stopover conservation efforts, researchers have built stopover habitat models for numerous parts of the Great Lakes watershed, based on extensive literature review and expert opinion (Byrne 2008, Bryan et al. 2011, Ewert et al. 2006, Grveles et al. 2011), but few if any studies have explicitly tested those models in the region.  The patterns of stopover use in the Lake Ontario watershed may differ from that in other portions of the Great Lakes because of the unique land cover patterns along NY’s Lake Ontario shore, particularly the southern shore where spring migrants might concentrate (more remaining natural cover, particularly bands of it farther inland than 4 km but still within the distance ranges correlated with migrant settlement patterns).  In addition, even larger areas of forest are intact within the Finger Lakes region, which may be within the distance from Lake Ontario in which birds have been shown to respond to major geographical features (Bonter et al. 2009, Diehl et al. 2003).  We do not know whether migrants are using these areas at similar rates to shoreline habitats.  Indeed, few studies of stopover patterns within the Great Lakes region have extended past 15 km of the shoreline, and they are all based on radar data.  These radar studies have provided good insight into patterns (Bonter et al. 2009, Buler and Dawson 2012, Diehl and Larkin 2003), but there are wide swaths of Lake Ontario’s watershed, particularly of the coastal areas, that are not covered by those data.  A previous study suggested that, as has been shown elsewhere in the Great Lakes, there were more birds within the first kilometer of the shoreline than 3‐4 km inland, but this trend was weak or absent along many sections of the shoreline and based only on spring migration data (Agard and Spellman 1994).  Given the increasing prominence and use of predictive models throughout the region and these spatial and temporal gaps in our understanding of stopover habitat use in the Great Lakes, more ground‐truthing is needed.

We developed hypotheses about stopover patterns in our area, tested them with data collected by skilled volunteers from a large study area during both spring and fall migrations to maximize the applicability of the results, and refined a predictive GIS model of stopover patterns for our region.  Here, we present the resulting spatial predictions of migrant abundance and richness across the southern portion of the Lake Ontario watershed in New York.  Our results are applicable to land birds that use forest and shrub cover, which are thought to be the most abundant land bird group migrating through the Great Lakes region compared to migrants characteristic of grasslands (Robertson et al. 2011) or wetlands (Meyer et al. 2010).  The spatial models we used to create the maps explain considerable variation in our data, and many features of the resulting maps are consistent with results from around the Great Lakes region.  Therefore, based upon these maps, we suggest areas for conservation focus.  We also make management recommendations in the user guide accompanying the predictive map portfolio, based on literature review and important predictors that we could not incorporate into the spatial model at the current time due to lack of sufficient consistent data across the region (i.e. habitat structure, vegetation composition).  Our hope is that these data will also help support and refine predictive models throughout the Great Lakes, including those being built for the entire region (Ewert et al. 2012) and all of NY State (Howard and Schlesinger in prep., Howard et al. in prep.).  These data will be useful for guiding conservation efforts, including anticipating potential consequences of projected climate change, siting of wind energy facilities, and other current and projected activities that could disproportionately affect large numbers of migrating birds near the Great Lakes’ shorelines.

## **Methods**

## **Study area**

We conducted the study along the southern shore of Lake Ontario in New York, extending south into the Finger Lakes region (Map 1).  All of the study area has been largely shaped by glacial processes.  The topography is diverse as the relatively flat lake plain along Lake Ontario transitions to the steep hills and north‐south running valleys of the Finger Lakes.  This area is a mix of forest, agriculture (primarily stone fruits and vegetable crops), and suburban and urban development, with development concentrated around the cities of Buffalo, Rochester and Syracuse.  We limited the study to the southern shoreline of Lake Ontario that runs roughly east‐west (Map 1) for several reasons.  First, a previous study showed fairly clearly that the eastern shore of Lake Ontario is used heavily by migrating birds (Agard and Spellman 1994), and most of the lands along that shoreline are currently protected and have been for some time, making further information about this area less critical.  Second, distance from the lake was easier to assess given the east‐west orientation of this shoreline; we could avoid trying to sort out the possible effects of birds piling up on that shoreline because they were flying around, rather than across the lake, and combining with birds just approaching the lake from the southeast.  Last, skilled volunteers were much more available for locations easily accessible from urban areas.  We further limited the study area to no closer than 60 km from Lake Erie, in order to avoid complications from the potentially interacting influences of both lakes on migrant behavior.

## **Study design**

We hypothesized that the number and diversity of migrants using a site for stopover would increase with 1) the amount of suitable habitat within the landscape and 2) proximity to Lake Ontario.  We stratified our sampling design based on these two factors, using thresholds shown to be relevant in other locations.  We used a moving window analysis of the 2001 National Land Cover Dataset (NLCD) 30‐m raster grid to establish the percent woody cover within a 5‐km radius of each cell.  The proportion of the landscape with suitable cover has been demonstrated to be the best metric for evaluating how the distribution of migrants is affected by the amount and distribution of habitat, including patchiness (Williams 2002, Bender et al. 2003, Tischendorf et al. 2003, Johnson 2012).  We selected a 5‐km radius as the size of the surrounding landscape for two reasons: settlement decisions seem to be correlated with land cover at this scale (Buler et al. 2007; Chernetsov 2006, Bonter et al. 2009), and it is at the top end of the range of post‐settlement movement distances for most land bird species (Aborn and Moore 1997, Cochran and Wikelski 2005, Matthews and Rodewald 2010, Ktitorov et al. 2010, MacDade et al. 2011, Seewagen et al. 2010, Slater 2011, references in Buler and Moore 2011; but see Buchanan 2008, Mills et al. 2011, Taylor et al. 2011 for species that travel farther post‐landing).

Since Lake Ontario ensures that sites close to the lakeshore have far fewer cells within that radius that _could_ be woody cover, we eliminated 30‐m cells that fell within the Lake Ontario boundary from the analysis.  We stratified our sampling approximately equally among the following: <20%, 20‐40%, and >40% woody cover within a 5‐km radius.  Studies suggest that sites with <10% of cover in the surrounding landscape may not be sufficient for mass gain (Kititorov et al. 2008), but there were not enough places in our study area to ensure replication (and relevance), so we increased the threshold to 20%, which is in the middle of the range that generally seems to affect bird and mammal distributions (Andrén 1994) and migrants in particular (Skagen et al. 1998, Somershoe and Chandler 2004).  Studies suggest that there is little difference in migrant abundance and richness above 40% cover in the landscape (Williams 2002 but see Buler et al. 2007), and the distribution of locations that could meet a greater threshold than 40% was limited to the Finger Lakes and eastern portions of the study area.

We evaluated proximity to Lake Ontario using the shortest distance to the shore from each 30‐m cell, and ensured there were replicates within the following distance bands:  <2 km, 2‐15 km, 15‐45 km, and 45‐60 km.

Sampling was weighted closer to Lake Ontario to maximize power to characterize the shape of the relationship between proximity and stopover use, as well as maximize our power to discriminate highly used sites from those less used within the coastal zone where competition for land use is high and property is expensive.  Many studies have shown a concentration of migrants along the shoreline.  A previous study around Lake Ontario showed that a marked decline (18%) in abundance was evident as little as 3 km from the shore (Agard and Spellman 1994).  Similar results were found along Lake Huron (Ewert et al. 2011).  Other studies have suggested that the effect of the Great Lakes might be evident at distances from 10 to 50 km as well (Bonter et al. 2009; Buler and Dawson 2012).  We selected 45 km as a conservative cutoff for all possible influence by Lake Ontario on stopover site selection; studies have shown that birds may reorient their flight pattern in response to barriers as much as 30 km from a barrier (Diehl et al. 2003).  Finally, to extend the study into the Finger Lakes, we set the study limit at 60 km.  This allowed us to explore how those water bodies and that area of largely intact forest cover might influence stopover habitat.  Distances beyond that were not easily covered by volunteers.

## **Sample site selection**

We piloted our sampling methods at 20 sites in Spring 2009 randomly selected from among woody cover patches that met each combination of percent woody cover within the landscape and distance from Lake Ontario, restricting our initial sampling to three narrow distance bands.  After this first season of data collection, we made several changes to our study design.  We increased the minimum amount of woody cover around each transect and made all transects a standard length, 300 m.  To standardize early morning sun exposure and inclusion of edge habitat, we placed all transects along an approximately east‐facing edge of a patch of woods. Pilot sites where the transect could not be modified to meet these criteria were abandoned, with the exception of two transects that ran nearly due west to due east; these were kept because both were along an edge with good sun exposure and additional permissions were hard to secure for sites near the lakeshore.

We assembled a GIS layer of all possible sites meeting the following criteria (see website and metadata for spatial package for more detail when available for more detail):

- contiguous woody cover (including deciduous, evergreen, and mixed forest; scrub/shrub; palustrine forested wetland and palustrine shrub/scrub wetland classes) sufficient to accommodate a 300 m x 50 m transect along an approximately eastern facing edge, with at least 150 m of additional woody cover along the interior edge of the transect,

- less than half a mile from a road (for ease of volunteer access and safety), and

- intersecting fewer than four tax parcels (to increase chances of securing permission to access the site).

This layer of approximately 1,500 suitable patches was then divided into twelve unique classes, one for each combination of proximity to Lake Ontario and % woody cover.  Approximately ten patches were selected randomly from within each class as candidate sampling sites and given further scrutiny.  Each was screened manually using satellite imagery to ensure that a 300‐m transect placed within it could meet the following criteria:

- along an approximately eastern facing edge (bearing no more than +/‐ 45 degrees from north‐south, with no more than a 45‐degree angle in the transect),

- less than 50% conifer and no conifer plantations,

- within woody cover (had not been harvested since the NLCD was assembled, not orchards or other misclassifications),

- far enough away from a major roadway (interstates and other known high traffic roads) so road noise would not interfere with bird detection,

- crossed fewer than three parcels.

Sites were randomly drawn until ten were identified that met all of these criteria for every combination. Contact information for the parcel owners was assembled from the tax data and landowners were contacted by letter.  In a few instances, sites with secured permission were abandoned because there was no safe volunteer access to the transect, the shrub layer was too impenetrable for volunteers to sample within the patch, the site was too wet for volunteers to access, or the adjacent road noise was too loud.  In cases where permissions were not secured for enough suitable sites for the classification from this set of ten, we identified public lands that met these criteria and secured permission.  Over the course of the study, a few sites were abandoned for an individual season or for the duration of the study due to excessive road and rail noise (1), logging at the site (1), flooding at the site (1), or difficulties getting volunteers to the site (3).  Sites were added, when possible, to replace those sites.  In total 71 transects were surveyed with data from 63 used for the final analyses.

Sample site locations are shown in Map 1, and the distribution of these sites across gradients of proximity to Lake Ontario and percent woody cover within the landscape is shown in Figure 1.

Transects were established approximately 25 m from the edge of woody cover, with the starting location determined by proximity to parking and ease of access.  Transects extended for 300 m approximately parallel to the edge of the woody cover, occasionally bending in order to maintain that course.  We also flagged the edges of the sampling area at the start, midpoint, and end of each transect.  A few transects had gaps in the middle due to treefalls, impenetrable thickets, or other hazards, but the total sampled area was equal for all transects.

## **Volunteers**

Volunteers were recruited by advertising for “experienced” birders, who were at least moderately comfortable birding by ear, in Audubon chapter newsletters, on birding email distribution lists, by word of mouth, and by active recruitment of individuals that staff or other volunteers thought were sufficiently skilled.  Volunteers were given a two‐hour orientation and training session at the beginning of each season, and provided with a volunteer manual detailing the sampling protocols and highlighting important things to remember.  Each volunteer took the same “quiz” to determine their ability (usually pre‐season, when their skills were rusty) to identify birds by sight and sound.  We designed the quiz to be difficult in order to get a wide spread of scores, which was more useful for analyzing whether or not birder score affected the response variables.  No one, not even our Audubon staff members and top birders, scored 100%.  While we did not exclude anyone from participating, we excluded data from volunteers scoring <40% on the combined sight and sound portions of the quiz, as these scores were lower than those of staff members who self‐identified as not skilled enough to collect data for the study.  We tried to ensure that volunteer score averaged out across a season at individual sites by arranging the schedule to ensure that all sites were sampled at least once by very good birders with high scores. By looking at the distribution of volunteer scores, and the average volunteer score across samples at a site within each season (Appendix A), we determined we were successful in accomplishing this.  See Appendix B for the quiz.

## **Migrant observations**

Sampling occurred for five to six weeks in each season, with spring sampling beginning the last week of April and ending in late May‐early June, and fall sampling beginning the first full week of September and continuing through mid‐October.  Based on banding data from the Braddock Bay Bird Observatory just west of Rochester, these time frames would capture at least 80%, and likely close to 90%, of species and individuals moving through our area (http://www.bbbo.org/, data received from D. Bonter).  Weeks were divided into two sampling periods, overlapping on Wednesday, and volunteers could sample any day within the designated sampling period.  We endeavored to sample each site at least five times during each migration season, and to have no more than two unsampled periods (equivalent to one week) in a row for a site.  A sample schedule is attached (Appendix C).  To ensure volunteer skill did not covary with site, each site was sampled by at least three

volunteers over the course of the season, and sampled no more than three times by the same individual.  Based on volunteer test scores, we also attempted to ensure each site was sampled overall by an average skill set, with moderate success (Appendix A).

Sampling was conducted between half an hour and four hours after sunrise in calm (wind <Beaufort scale 4), fairly dry (no more than a sprinkle), and good visibility (no fog) conditions.  When there were not suitable conditions within a sampling period, but the data point was needed to ensure enough samples at that site, occasional exceptions were granted.

Volunteers walked along the flagged 300‐m transects in 30 minutes and counted and identified all birds seen and/or heard within 25 meters on either side of the transect (Fig. 2).  Birds judged to be flying over the transect but not actively foraging or landing were not included.  Volunteers then returned to the transect midpoint and played a five‐minute recording of chickadees mobbing a screech owl (the same track used by Cornell Birds in Forested Landscapes, http://www.birds.cornell.edu/bfl/, from the Macaulay Library of Natural Sounds).  They counted and identified all birds seen and heard at close range, responding to that recording, both while it was playing and for five minutes afterward.  Volunteers were urged to record individuals as unknown if they were not fairly positive of the identification, and were allowed but not encouraged to “stop the clock” in order to try to get closer to a bird to verify its identity.  Volunteer instructions and elements from the notebook given to each volunteer, for privacy reasons not including transect locations and associated details, are attached (Appendix D).

Most volunteers submitted data throughout the season by e‐mailing data entry forms that were coded for easy upload into our database.  The rest were submitted in hard copy at the end of the season.  Data was screened for whether they were collected at the right time of day and the transect walked for no more than 40 minutes (compared to the requested 30).  We also checked the data for any unusual observations (unexpected species, unusual numbers of rare species, or unusually high numbers of any species) and verified them with the observer and with Audubon staff before incorporating them into the database.  Unknowns were grouped (see Appendix H).  Most necessary edits were essentially copy editing the data.  Based on entered data, virtually all submitted data met the basic criteria of being collected and recorded correctly, and there were very few observations deemed “unlikely” and removed from the dataset.

## **Transect habitat predictors**

Tree characteristics were assessed at four locations along each transect, 30 m, 110 m, 190 m, and 270 m, consisting of a tree plot and two shrub plots on either side of the transect (Figure 2).  Tree species and diameter at breast height were recorded for all trees located within a variable radius plot established by a factor 10 sampling prism.  Average height of the canopy was estimated by measuring the heights of three trees with a clinometer.  Shrub layer characteristics were assessed in eight 2‐m diameter circular plots within the transect, centered 12.5 m on either side of the tree plots.  We estimated total percent cover of shrubs within three height layers (0.5‐2.5 m, 2.5‐5.0 m, and above 5 m) and also counted stems by species within each of those layers. Additionally, we characterized ground cover within these shrub plots, estimating the percent cover of grasses, forbs, woody seedlings, bare ground, leaf litter, and woody debris.  Canopy cover was estimated using a convex spherical densiometer at twelve points within each transect, including at all four tree plots and all eight shrub plots.  Vertical structure was estimated at these twelve points as well, counting the number of branches intersecting a (virtual) vertical cylinder above the sampling point and the number of height classes with structure above that point (2‐4, 4‐8. 8‐16, 16‐32, 32+ m).  Slope and aspect were measured at each of the four tree plots.  These compositional and structural characteristics have been correlated with migratory and/or breeding bird abundance or richness (Deppe and Rotenberry 2008, Rodewald and Brittingham 2004, Rodewald

and Matthews 2005, Suthers et al. 2000), and our methods for determining these habitat characteristics were modified from these studies and common forestry metrics.

## **Landscape predictors**

We calculated the shortest distance to the shoreline of Lake Ontario using Euclidean distance, as well as the shortest distance to Lake Ontario excluding the large bays (Irondequoit, Sodus, Little Sodus, and Port Bays). Since the Finger Lakes and other linear inland lakes may provide food as well as navigational aids during migration, we also included distance to embayments and lakes as a predictor (see Appendix G for list). Additional predictors including elevation, latitude, and longitude were also included because patterns of topography and land cover use vary noticeably west and east of Rochester, with greater patchiness and isolation in the flat agricultural landscapes west of Rochester and more heterogeneity of cover amidst the drumlin fields east of Rochester.

We characterized the percent cover of land use at varying distances (500, 1,000, 5,000 and 10,000 m) from the transect center point using moving window analyses of the Coastal Change Analysis Program (CCAP) land cover dataset, simplified to seven cover types (open water, wetland, forest, shrub, agriculture, urban, barren land). We also assessed percent cover of these cover types within a 75‐m buffer of the transect center line.  Percent canopy cover within 500, 1,000 and 5,000 m from the transect center point was also calculated using the 2001 National Land Cover Dataset canopy layer.  We characterized the variety of habitat around each transect using the number of woody cover types (deciduous, evergreen and mixed forest; scrub/shrub; palustrine forested wetland; and palustrine scrub/shrub wetland) found within 500 and 1,000 m of the transect center.  We calculated the density of roads (km of road per square kilometer), weighted by speed limit, within 500, 1,000, and 5,000 m of the transect center.

Finally, we included several other habitat fragmentation related variables that might affect migrant distribution, and assessed them using 1,000 m moving window analyses rather than patch‐centric analyses for consistency with the other predictors and because there is little evidence that “patches” are a more meaningful construct for migrant decisions than the landscape as a whole.  So, within 1,000 m of the transect center (or raster cell, for the predictive model), we characterized, using FragStats 4.0 (McGarigal et al. 2012):  1) average area of patches, both weighted by proportion in the landscape and non‐weighted; 2) edge density; 3) total length of edge (where edge was contrast between woody and non woody cover, rather than among all cover types); 4) patch density (number of patches divided by the area of the 1,000 m radius circle, so essentially a measure of fragmentation within the immediate surroundings); and 5) gyration (average distance between each cell in a patch and the patch centroid, a combination of patch area and patch compactness), both weighted by proportion in the landscape and non‐weighted.

All predictors are summarized in Appendix G.

## **Analysis**

To better understand migration behavior through the study area, we limited our analyses to individuals most likely to be migrating through and not stopping to breed.  We created nested subsets of species based on a) whether or not they were migratory and b) the likelihood that a species would be breeding in the area, based on the number of records of breeding individuals within the study area (McGowan and Corwin 2008) and the breeding range of the species (http://www.allaboutbirds.org/Page.aspx?pid=1189, based on Ridgely et al. 2003). Non‐migrants were excluded from all analyses.  We created three groups of migrants:

1) Group 1 ‐ _Migrants:_ species nearly certain to be using a site in our area for stopover and not breeding (<3% of the atlas blocks in the study area with breeding records, and at least half of the breeding range north of the study area);

2) Group 2 ‐ _Likely migrants:_ species likely to be stopping over and not breeding (<25% of atlas blocks in the study area with breeding records, and at least half of the breeding range north of the study area); and

3) Group 3 ‐ _Breeders:_ species that could be breeding in the study area (common local breeder OR rare local breeder but most of range is to the south of the study area) (species groups in Appendix E).

The locations and timing of the observations for close to half of the individuals for group 2, the likely migrants, suggested that they were migrating, not breeding, at those locations, so results shown in this report are for groups 1 and 2 combined.  Results for group 1 alone were similar.  Any marked differences are explained in the results section.

Migrant species richness was calculated using the number of unique species observed at a site on each sampling date, including both transect and mobbing data.  Transect abundance data and mobbing abundance data were kept separate to avoid double counting individuals and reduce possible bias because some species responded to the mobbing call more than others.

To reduce between‐sample error introduced by variation in the number of samples per transect per season and different temporal distributions of samples among sites due to volunteer availability, we bootstrapped the data (resampling 1,000 times within an individual sampling season, with replacement).  Any transects that were not sampled at least four times within a season and data collected by volunteers with a quiz score less than 40% were excluded.

To determine important predictors of migrant richness and abundance and to develop spatial predictions of stopover habitat use across our study area, we used regression random forests.  A random forest is a machine learning technique, an ensemble classifier that consists of many decision trees and outputs the class that is the mode (classification, like trees voting) or average (regression) of the classes output by individual trees. Each tree in the forest is built using a randomly selected bootstrap sample of the data, and each node in the tree is determined by a random subset of the given predictors.  Thousands of these trees are built, creating a “forest.” Random forests have several advantages useful for handling this dataset: 1) they can handle small sample sizes relative to the number of predictors, high order interactions, and correlated and/or noisy predictor variables; 2) they do not overfit; 3) there are methods for generating variable importance measures, which were important to us for explaining the predictions (more below); and 4) outputs can be used to generate dissimilarity matrices & multi‐dimensional scaling plots, creating a visualization of which transects often appeared near each other on terminal nodes.  Variable importance in random forests is assessed by randomly permuting the values for a given predictor variable for the out‐of‐ bag observations, and then those modified out‐of‐bag data are passed down the tree to get new predictions (Liaw and Wiener 2002, Cutler et al. 2007).

We built random forest (RF) models using the randomForest package (Liaw and Wiener 2002, version 4.6‐6) for R statistical software (R Development Core Team 2006), based on the original Fortran code by Breiman and Cutler (Breiman 2001, http://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~breiman/RandomForests/).  We tuned the models using the tuneRF option with the randomForest package to determine the number of variables tried at each split that would minimize the out‐of‐bag error estimate, and used sufficient trees in the forest so that both the error estimate and the order of importance for the predictor variables stabilized (100,000 trees for most response variables, but stable consistency of the most important variables was achieved with far fewer).  Since we hypothesized that the best predictors would differ between spring and fall, we built separate random forests for spring and fall using data from only those seasons.  Code for the random forests and associated plots is in Appendix F.

## **Prediction maps**

We used regression random forests built using only the predictors that we could translate into a GIS framework to predict a value for every 30x30‐m grid cell within the study area.  Again, we ran the predictions using separate random forests built from spring species richness data, spring transect abundance data, fall species richness data, and fall transect abundance data, as described above.  As above, we selected values for mtry (the number of predictors to use to determine each split in each tree in the forest) that minimized the out‐of‐bag error estimate, used 50,000 trees for each prediction (more for spatial prediction bogged the senior author’s computer down), and ran the predictions using the predict package within R (code is in Appendix F).

We then screened out all cells that were not suitable habitat, based on the selection criteria we used to screen the study sites to begin with, leaving only predicted pixels classed within the CCAP 2006 layer as deciduous, evergreen and mixed forest; scrub/shrub; palustrine forested wetland; or palustrine scrub/shrub wetland.  Since we limited our sampling to patches large enough to fit a transect, and since very small patches of habitat may not make effective targets for conservation action, we further screened out cells that were in clusters smaller than 80 pixels (our minimum sampling area was approximately 300 m x 250 m).

## **Results**

## **Summary**

- For the ten most abundance species in our dataset (migrant groups 1 and 2 combined), our dataset captures at least 28% (average 88%) of the range of interannual variability of spring migration and at least 68% (average 112%) of the range of interannual variability of fall migration.

- Variations in volunteer ability do not drive the other results (Appendix A).

- Random forests were able to explain 26‐50% of the variation in average richness and average abundance at a site per season.  The amounts were surprisingly similar for spring and fall, and greater for species richness than for abundance (Table 2).

- Landscape scale predictors were most important in the spring; transect habitat predictors (namely shrub cover, stem density, and fruiting shrub richness) were as or more important than landscape scale predictors in fall (Figures 5 & 6).

- Both species richness and abundance of migrants and likely migrants declined markedly with increasing distance from Lake Ontario’s shoreline in both spring and fall; the decline was steeper in the spring (Figure 7).

- Migrant abundance and richness was positively correlated with the amount of urban cover and the density of roads in the surrounding landscape, even more so than with the amount of woody cover in the landscape (Figure 11).

- These habitat “islands” within an urban matrix were more used close to Lake Ontario than far from the shoreline (Figure 11).

- Shrub cover, stem density, and fruiting shrub species richness were strongly positively correlated with both spring and fall responses, and at least one of those shrub‐related predictors was an important one in the random forest for each response (Figures 5 & 6, Appendix G).

- Although not a prominent predictor in the random forests, the variety of cover types within the surrounding landscape (up to 1000m) was also positively correlated with richness and abundance in both seasons (Figures 5 & 6, Appendix G).

## **Complete Results**

We observed over 50,000 birds of 159 species over the course of 1,385 site visits.  Over 7,000 of the individuals we observed within the boundary of the transect itself were quite likely to be migrating through the area (migrants and likely migrants, individuals from migrant groups 1 and 2, see Appendix E for a breakdown), and species from these groups were recorded at all sites.  Fifty‐five volunteers collectively logged more than 2,000 hours over the course of the project to collect and help process these data.

As expected, there was considerable year‐to‐year variation in the migrations (Figures 3 & 4, Table 1).  Spring 2010 was fairly dry with temperatures much above normal in the northeastern U.S., but closer to normal in the southeastern U.S., whereas spring 2011 was unusually wet with above normal temperatures, both within our ‐ ‐ ‐ region and across much of the eastern half of the U.S. (http://climvis.ncdc.noaa.gov/cgi bin/cag3/state map display.pl).  Indeed, in spring 2011 the volunteers had difficulty birding at several sites because they were knee to waist deep in water in the first part of the season, whereas we had established them the year before with no suspicion that conditions like that were possible.  Fall 2010 had unusually high numbers of migrants and higher migrant richness, partly driven by the number of white throated sparrows.  Braddock Bay Bird Observatory (BBBO) banded twice as many of these sparrows in 2010 as they did in 2009 and 2011 (data from D. Bonter, www.bbbo.org ).  When we compared the coefficients of variation for the number of birds banded by BBBO across the years we sampled to the coefficients of variation across the entire 13 year dataset, we captured approximately 20% of the interannual variation among springs and 120% of the interannual variation across falls, summing across all migrant species.  When we looked at the ten most abundant species in our dataset from migrant groups 1 and 2 combined, our dataset captures an average of 88% (minimum 28%)) of the range of interannual variability of spring migration and an average of 112% (minimum 68%) of the range of interannual variability of fall migration.

Average ability of volunteers (as indicated by volunteer quiz scores, see Methods and Appendices 1 & 2) sampling a site across a season did positively correlate with species richness and abundance for the most restricted subset of migrants used for the analyses included in this report, but the correlation coefficients were less than those of the most important predictors (correlation coefficients: spring richness =0.29, fall richness=0.26, spring abundance 0.32, fall abundance 0.02) (Appendix G).  In random forests that were built using each individual observation and “within sample” sources of variation as predictors (observer quiz score, year, week, day, time, and volunteer score), observer quiz score was not the most important variable, and explained similar amounts of variation as day of the year.  Most importantly, average ability of volunteers sampling at a site did not co‐vary with any of the major predictors, and its variable importance value was never greater than that explained by random variation (greater than the absolute value of the most negative importance value—negative importance values are meaningless).  Consequently, differences in volunteer ability likely do not drive any of the other results.

For the most restricted set of migrants (group 1), the random forest models using between‐site predictors explained 26‐50% of the variation in average richness and average abundance at a site per season.  The models explained more of the variation in species richness than abundance, but the amounts were surprisingly similar for spring and fall (49.16% and 28.93% for spring richness and abundance, respectively, and 42.02% and 28.72% for fall richness and abundance) (Table 2).  Including “likely migrants” as well as the “migrants” (groups 1 & 2) increased the amount of variation in abundance that was explained, but reduced the amount of variation in richness that was explained (Table 2).  Since the results were similar, and the dataset combining the two groups is nearly twice the size as that for just group 1, increasing our confidence in the results, all figures and maps shown in this report are for migrant groups 1 and 2 combined.  Despite considerable variation among years, random forests built from individual seasons, rather than averaging across years, had similar rankings of

important predictor variables but explained slightly less variation (21‐34%, data not shown).  Consequently, we present results for models that average across years.

Figures 5 and 6 show the importance of the predictors for each of the response variables ranked in descending order using two different metrics.  The first, percent increase in mean square error, is the average difference between the mean square error for trees constructed using the real data for that predictor and the mean square error for trees constructed using randomly permuted versions of that predictor that are passed down the tree, normalized by the standard deviation of the differences.  The second metric is the total decrease in node impurities (residual sum of squares) from splitting on the variable, averaged across all trees in the forest (from randomForest package documentation, http://127.0.0.1:10723/library/randomForest/html/importance.html). Although the rank was not exactly the same for both metrics, the sets of the top ten or so were usually equivalent.

In the spring, landscape‐scale predictors, rather transect habitat predictors, explained the majority of the variation in abundance and richness (Figure 5).  Indeed, random forest models built using transect habitat predictors only were so poor they did not model better than random variation (results not shown).  Greater numbers and species of birds were found closer to Lake Ontario, and distance from the lake as well as variables strongly correlated with it (latitude, elevation, % of open water in a large radius) were most important within the random forests.  Richness and abundance declined steeply within the first few kilometers from the shoreline and were nearly constant beyond ten kilometers (Figure 7a, b).  Urban cover and road density were also important predictors, particularly for abundance, and were actually positively correlated with migrant richness and abundance.  Urban cover within a 5,000‐m radius had a step‐like relationship with migrants, with apparent thresholds at 10%, 20%, and 60% (Figure 8b).  The effect of road density was similarly step‐like (Figure 9b). These predictors might be thought of as “degree of isolation” surrogates, and explained more of the variation in abundance than in richness.  They were also even more important predictors for the most restricted set of migrants (results not shown).  Finally, agricultural cover within a 5,000‐m radius was negatively correlated with both richness and abundance, but a more important predictor for abundance.  Landscapes this size (5,000‐m radius) with more than 35% agricultural cover had fewer individuals and fewer species of birds than those with < 35% agricultural cover (Figure 10a,b).

In the fall, the most restricted set of migrants was best predicted by a combination of both local and landscape scale predictors: shrub cover and density within the understory (positive correlation), elevation (negative correlation), and correlates with distance from the lake, including latitude and distance from the shoreline excluding bays (negative correlation) (Figure 6).  For abundance, but not richness, urban cover and road density were important positive predictors.  Tree basal area (positively correlated with the number of large trees in this dataset, correlation coefficient 0.75) was negatively correlated and a moderately important predictor for richness, but not abundance.  Although, as in spring, greater numbers and species of birds were found close to Lake Ontario, the slope of the relationship was more gradual (Figure 7c,d) out to approximately 8 km, and the distance predictors were less important, particularly for species richness.  For species richness in the fall, random forests including only the transect habitat predictors explained almost as much of the variation in the data as forests using all predictors (33.65% vs 41.43% variation explained for most restricted set of migrants, results not shown).  Fall abundance, however, was not explained by these habitat predictors alone (variation explained did not exceed that of random variation, results not shown).  Results were similar for the most restricted subset of migrants, with the additional important predictors of longitude and shrub cover within the landscape (in addition to that within the transect), and basal area not an important predictor for fall richness.

Interestingly, contrary to what we hypothesized, the amount of woody cover in the landscape was not among the most important predictors in the random forest models, and correlation strength was low.  Instead, the

amount of urban cover and road density were important positive correlates in the spring, as well as to a lesser extent in the fall.

There was a significant interaction between distance from the lake and the degree of isolation.  For instance, negative correlations between migrants and the amount of woody cover within the larger landscape (1km and greater) were strong close to the lake (<5km), but hovered around zero farther from the lake (>5km) (Figure 11). The interaction between distance from the lake and isolation was particularly marked for fall abundance, which was positively correlated with road density and urban cover assessed over small neighborhoods close to the lake, but had virtually no correlation beyond five kilometers from the lake (Figure 11).  For the most restricted set of migrants (group 1), positive correlations between abundance and richness and the amount of urban cover and road density in the landscape were considerably greater closer to the lake (<5km) than farther from it (>5km) in both seasons (Figure 11). However this was not evident when likely migrants (group 2) were also included.  Similarly, negative correlations with agricultural cover, particularly in the spring, were also more marked close to the lake.  When these interactions (woody cover, urban cover, and road density crossed with distance from the lake) were included as predictors in the random forest, one was in the top seven predictors for all four response variables, and the woody cover*distance interaction was the most important predictor of spring richness (results not shown).

Of the various landscape scales we included among the predictors (75, 500, 1,000, 5,000, 10,000‐m radii around the transect), larger landscape contexts were generally more strongly correlated with migrant abundance and richness than immediate surroundings, with a few exceptions (Appendix G for full correlation matrix).  For example, in the fall, close to the lake, urban cover and road density within the immediate surroundings of the transect were more strongly correlated with abundance than urban cover and road density assessed over larger neighborhoods (Figure 11, Appendix G).  Shrub cover and agricultural cover were both most strongly correlated with richness and abundance in both seasons when assessed using a 1,000 m radius or less (Appendix G).

Among the transect habitat predictors, shrub‐related predictors (percent cover of shrubs and species richness and stem density of all shrubs or fruiting shrubs) were among the most strongly positively correlated with both richness and abundance in the fall (Appendix G).  Shrub cover within the lowest layer of the understory (0.5‐2 m) was particularly strongly correlated with richness and abundance in both seasons, and was an important predictor in the random forests for the fall (Figures 5&6).  Although it was a much less important predictor in the spring, its importance value was still greater than could be explained by random variation.  In the fall, abundance and richness were negatively correlated with structural variables that probably reduce shrub cover, including the basal area within the variable radius tree plots, tree species richness, the number of large trees, the variety of tree sizes, and vertical complexity in the upper canopy (Appendix G).  In contrast, spring richness and abundance were positively correlated with the number of large trees in the transect.  Steeper slopes also had more migrants in the spring, but not in the fall.  Diversity of the ground cover was positively correlated with responses in both seasons, and the percent of ground cover that was leaf litter (as opposed to vegetation, woody debris, water, or bare ground) was positively correlated with species richness in both the spring and the fall, but these were never important predictors within the random forests.

## **Predictive models**

Random forests constructed using only the landscape‐scale predictors explained similar amounts of variation in the spring migration as the full models did, but explained less of the variation in the fall migration data (compare Table 3 to Table 2).  The model for fall richness of migrant groups 1 and 2 combined explained much less variation than the models for the other responses, but predicted the real values comparably well (Figure 14, R[2] =0.83).  The fall richness model for solely the most restricted set of migrants, group 1, performed fairly well (Table 3).  Results for solely group 1 are available upon request, or refer to Map11 to see how the predictions for

the two sets differed.  The rank orders of variable importance for spring and fall are shown in Figures 12 and 13, respectively.  All models tended to over predict values at the lower end of the scale and under predict the top values, so the spatial predictions of the highest value areas are likely conservative, and low value areas may be of even less value than indicated (Figure 14, R[2] =0.83‐0.87).

Distance from Lake Ontario and its strong correlates, as well as urban cover and road density within the surrounding landscape, were the most important predictors of species richness and abundance in the spring (Figure 12).  There are hotspots on the maps along most of the Lake Ontario shoreline as well as a wide ring of predicted high abundance around the major cities, but particularly around Rochester.  Inland wetland complexes (Montezuma and Iroquois‐Tonawanda‐Oak Orchard Wetland Complexes) and large intact forest areas between the Finger Lakes are predicted to have moderately high species richness and abundance inland (Maps 3 and 4). Richness and abundance are predicted to decline steeply up to 5 km from the Lake, but richness was predicted to be slightly elevated as far inland as 15 km, compared to sites farther away (Figure 15a).  Multi‐dimensional scaling plots generated using dissimilarity matrices from the random forests show that the forests discriminate the best sites very well, splitting them into two groups that roughly correspond to those isolated within urban and suburban matrices and those in a mixed agricultural and forest matrix (Figure 16a,b).

Interestingly, for the most restricted set of migrants, spring abundance patterns were less well explained by the random forest than richness, and there was considerably more scatter in the dissimilarity matrices (data not shown).  For this restricted set of migrants, isolation related predictors (road density and urban cover within the landscape) were more important than distance from the lake, and this is apparent on the map (data available upon request, see also Map 10).  Intact forest areas within the Finger Lakes region and larger patches of forest within 15 km of the shoreline in the eastern edge of the study area are less prominent on the predictive maps using only this most restricted set of migrants (Map 10).

As mentioned above, the predictive spatial models for fall explained less variation than did those for spring. Sites closer to Lake Ontario as well as those with higher shrub cover in the surrounding landscape were predicted to have greater species richness.  For fall richness, urban cover and road density were less important than in spring, and this is apparent on the maps as areas around Rochester are considerably less prominent.  In the predictive model that used landscape‐scale variables only, fall species richness declined with increasing distance from Lake Ontario, but not markedly until approximately 8 km (Figure 15c).  Therefore, the band of predicted high richness along the shore of Lake Ontario is wider on the fall migration maps.  There is also a greater area of predicted high richness in isolated inland wooded patches in the agricultural matrix west of Rochester, particularly in Wyoming County (Map 5).

Predicted fall abundance patterns were slightly more similar to spring abundance patterns than were species richness patterns.  The predicted band of high fall abundance along Lake Ontario is wider than in spring, but not nearly as wide as for fall richness (Figure 15d, Map 6), and the inland agricultural matrix areas are not as prominent for abundance as for richness (Map 6).  However, in this model, migrants are not predicted to use intact forest areas in the Finger Lakes region in the fall, in contrast with spring (compare Map 6 to Map 4).

For the fall, the primary differences between maps for the most restricted set of migrants compared with migrant groups 1 and 2 are 1) less prominence of areas around Montezuma, the Finger Lakes, and the eastern half of the study area, particularly within 20 km from Lake Ontario and 2) more prominence of woody cover in the agricultural areas in the western portion of Wyoming County as well as the band of woody cover approximately 20 km inland in the western portion of the study area (Maps 11 and 12).

To create a map showing these four responses combined, we took all points with a value greater than one standard deviation above the mean from the predicted distribution for each response.  See Appendix G for the

predicted distributions with mean and standard deviations marked.  We then rescaled each response from zero to one and then added the layers together (Map 7).  Note that pixels on this map could achieve a high value (orange to orange red) by having a high value for one response and just making the standard deviation cutoff for the other responses, but to have a very high value (red), a site needed to markedly exceed the standard deviation cutoff of more than one response.  Map 8 shows for which combination of response variables each pixel met the cutoff.

Overall, the models predict higher migrant richness and abundance in both seasons within a few kilometers of Lake Ontario in both spring and fall migrations, and up to eight kilometers inland in the fall.  Areas with natural cover within and around Iroquois‐Tonawanda‐Oak Orchard and Montezuma Wetland Complexes also “pop” on this combined map, and were important in both seasons, although a much greater total area around these refuges is predicted to be important in the fall.  Isolated patches of woody cover within urban and suburban matrices near Lakes Ontario and Erie are also associated with higher abundance and richness of migrants in spring and fall, but the rings of predicted high abundance and richness around Rochester and Buffalo are much wider for the spring.

## **Discussion**

Although land bird migration is notoriously variable (Mehlman et al. 2005, Moore et al. 2005), the predictive models used to create the maps included in this report explained considerable amounts of variation in the data and had low out‐of‐bag error estimates, with the exception of fall richness.  Models were fairly similar for migrants and likely migrants, but quite different when breeders were included (results not shown).  Along with field sampling timed during known migration windows, this result increases our confidence that these patterns truly reflect stopover and not breeding habitat, are applicable to many migratory land bird species, and are not spurious.  The models are also built from more than a single season, and they incorporate considerable interannual variation: two springs were sampled for nearly every site included in the analysis, and two falls for approximately half of the sites included.  For the ten most abundance species in our dataset (migrant groups 1 and 2 combined), our dataset captures at least 28% (average 88%) of the range of interannual variability of spring migration and at least 68% (average 112%) of the range of interannual variability of fall migration, based on Braddock Bay Bird Observatory banding data.  When tested on the real data, the models underpredicted sites with the highest abundance and richness, and overpredicted sites with the lowest abundance and richness (common for random forests), so if anything our models, and the gradients displayed on the predictive maps, are conservative renderings of true patterns of stopover habitat use.

These results show that migrants in our study area are clearly concentrated along the southern shores of Lake Ontario, as has been shown for parts of other Great Lakes (Ewert et al. 2011, Grveles 1998, Hyde 1998, Rodewald 2007), as well as hypothesized and modeled throughout the Great Lakes (Bryan et al. 2007, Byrne 2008, Ewert et al. 2006, Grveles et al. 2011).  Furthermore, we show that migrants use these coastal areas in both spring and fall migrations.  In the fall, migrants seem to spread out over a wider band around the Lake, using areas farther inland, but richness and abundance still drop off noticeably beyond 8 km from the shoreline. Potential habitat within the immediate coastal zone (within 2 km of the shoreline) was nearly uniformly predicted to have high migrant richness and abundance in both seasons, and therefore all potential habitat within this band appears as very high potential value on the combined map (Map 7).  Note that our on‐the‐ ground data show that within a season, there are at least some coastal sites with low abundance and richness of migrants, comparable to what we found at the majority of sites farther inland.  The trends and the spatial model are driven, in part, by considerably higher values of abundance and richness at coastal sites than the highest values at inland sites, even though low abundance and richness of migrants were found at some coastal sites in

some seasons (Figures 2 & 3, Table 1).  But very few, if any, of the sites in the coastal zone failed to stand out in at least one season in one year (Map 2).

Wooded areas isolated within a matrix of development in urban and suburban areas, or on the outskirts, were also predicted to have high migrant abundance and richness.  The effect of isolation was more predominant during spring migration.  In the spring, urban cover and road density were more important predictors (Figure 5) and had stronger correlation coefficients (Figure 11).  This can be seen in the predicted maps, particularly Map 8, which shows which areas were important in spring, fall, and/or both seasons.  Although urban cover and road density were important positive predictors of migrant richness and abundance in both seasons when assessed across the whole dataset, they were the top predictors when considering only sites within 5 km of the shoreline (results not shown).  However, note that the distribution of high intensity development in our study area is largely concentrated near the Great Lakes (Buffalo on Lake Erie, Rochester on Lake Ontario‐‐Syracuse was just east of the study area), and all of our sampling sites surrounded by urban cover were around Rochester, which also has other water features that might attract migrants (the Genesee River, Irondequoit Bay).  Therefore, “hotspots” around other small cities and large villages inland should be interpreted with caution and ideally verified through observation or other data sources (e.g., eBird).  However, other studies have also found higher concentrations of migrants within isolated habitat patches, including radar studies in our region (Williams 2002, Bonter et al. 2009, Buler and Dawson 2012).

Isolation seems to be less important farther from the coastal zone, however, and beyond 15‐20 km, there may be no effect (Figures 2, 3, & 11).  Interactions between distance from Lake Ontario and woody cover, urban cover and road density were very important predictors when included explicitly in the random forests.  Negative correlations with woody cover in the surrounding landscape were strong near the lake, but absent far from it, and positive correlations with urban cover and road density were weaker farther from the lake for the most restricted set of migrants.  (Random forests are adept at handling interactions without explicit incorporation of the interaction terms as predictors, but to determine their importance, we ran forests with these included explicitly).  This interaction is similar to what Buler and Moore (2011) noted on the Gulf Coast, where migrants land exhausted in the spring, and stop before the large barrier in the autumn, the opposite of our study area. There, close to the shore, birds are less closely associated with the amount of suitable habitat in the landscape in both spring and fall, though much more in the spring when having just crossed the Gulf, suggesting that after crossing, migrants are under strong pressures to land to rest, and may then be more selective at their next stop. We found the interaction in both seasons, perhaps because our study area is considerably more urbanized than theirs.

We found, as Bonter et al. (2009) did, that spring migrants were generally strongly negatively correlated with agriculture in the landscape, in contrast to a positive correlation with developed cover, particularly when considering a large landscape context (5‐10km).  However, in the fall, migrants were actually positively correlated with agricultural cover in that size landscape close to Lake Ontario, and correlations hovered around zero more than 5 km from Lake Ontario (Figure 11).  This interaction between landscape cover and distance from the Lake is similar to that discussed in the preceding paragraph, and may reflect that, particularly close to the shoreline, when migrants may need to rest after crossing Lake Ontario and perhaps cannot be choosy, migrants are using isolated wooded patches in the agricultural expanse between Buffalo and Rochester.

_**Where, then, should conservation efforts be focused?**_ First, we want to emphasize that most evidence, including ours, suggests that land birds migrate in a fairly broad front, and that a diffuse network of stopover habitat is needed throughout the region.  This is a daunting task, since only 0.6% (38,039 acres out of 6,314,870 acres) of the most important areas (colored areas on Maps 7 and 8) are currently under some form of protection.

With that caveat, our study, in combination with others, suggests that there are several areas that are highly used and/or of high value to migrating land birds:

_**1) Coastal zone.**_ Although we had hoped that results from this study would allow us to better discriminate among coastal areas to focus stopover conservation work in the highly developed and expensive coastal zone, our data suggest that all potential habitat that is left within the coastal zone (a fraction of what used to exist) may be used heavily at least in some years.  Within the coastal zone, as elsewhere, shrub cover between 0.5 and 2 m above the ground, shrub stem density, and fruiting shrub richness were all strongly correlated with abundance and richness in both the spring and the fall, and were very important predictors in the fall. Conservation and management of areas that do or could provide this type of shrubby habitat would be particularly beneficial for migratory birds.

_**2) Potential habitat isolated within a developed matrix, particularly within 5 km of Lake Ontario.**_ Areas with more than 10% urban cover in the surrounding landscape, or landscapes where less than 20% of the area is suitable habitat, will likely draw higher concentrations of migrants.  Does a concentration of migrants indicate importance?  What would happen if these isolated patches were not there?  Migrants might simply travel farther along the shoreline or inland to the next available patch.  However, at least within 5 km from Lake Ontario in the spring, the strength of the correlation between migrant richness and abundance increased with the size of the neighborhood we evaluated.  This might suggest that the more development there is within a 10‐ km radius, the more likely birds are to use the limited available habitat within that area, regardless of its size or quality.  Others have suggested that birds do indeed concentrate within these “fire escapes” (might be too low quality to refuel at) and “convenience stores” (offer moderate quality in an unsuitable habitat matrix), as termed by Mehlman et al. (2005), or habitat islands within matrices of developed or agricultural cover (Bonter et al. 2009, Brawn and Stotz, 2001; Buler and Dawson 2012, Seewagen and Slayton 2008).  If birds are piling up along the lake shore because they are caught out over the lake at dawn, as radar data suggest (Diehl et al. 2003), the extra energy to travel farther might have fitness costs (Petit 2000).  We think, therefore, that isolated sites within this zone are likely important stopover habitat and should be a focus of conservation, as others have suggested (Buler and Dawson 2012, many others).  We suggest that on‐the‐ground evaluations of habitat quality, evaluation of threats to existing available habitat, co‐benefits for other species, and opportunity should also be considered when focusing conservation within this zone.

_**3) Inland forest and wetland complexes.**_ Montezuma and Iroquois‐Tonawanda‐Oak Orchard Wetland Complexes clearly stand out on the map of places predicted to have high abundance and/or richness in both spring and fall (Maps 7 and 8).  Many of the other small inland areas that appear on this map as important in one or both seasons also have a wetland component.  In our models, this is likely driven by the importance of the amount of water within the surrounding landscape, which is not just due to the prominent effect of Lake Ontario, and likely the moderate importance of the variety of cover within the landscape.  Wetlands, water sources, and variety of habitat have all been previously suggested as elements that attract migrants and/or improve stopover habitat quality (Nicholls et al. 2001), and the former two are being included in a regional stopover habitat model (Ewert et al. 2012).

_**4) Potential habitat isolated within an agricultural matrix for many kilometers, particularly if it offers good food sources in the fall.**_ Our data support this less strongly than sites isolated within a developed matrix, but there are some areas in western Wyoming County that stand out like for this reason, and the wetland complexes discussed above may also be important because they are large diverse areas of suitable habitat within fairly inhospitable agricultural matrices.
