Remember, we found, as others have, that agricultural cover was negatively correlated with migrant abundance and richness in the spring, but we also found that it was slightly positively correlated with fall migrant activity.

_**5) Areas of fairly intact forest cover in the Finger Lakes region.**_ These areas clearly stand out on the included maps for the spring, but not the fall, and the pattern is much stronger for migrants and likely migrants combined than for solely migrants (Maps 9 & 10).  Looking at the individual sites and responses potentially driving this pattern, we are fairly sure it is not due solely, or even primarily, to the inclusion of species that might be breeding there.  Proximity to water is certainly important in our model, and not entirely driven by importance of Lake Ontario (the shapes of the partial plots for the percentage cover of water in the landscape do not tightly mirror those for distance from Lake Ontario (data not shown).  Others have found proximity to smaller lakes, rivers, and open water wetlands important (Bonter et al. 2009, Nicholls et al. 2001).  However, if this were the sole driver, the area between Honeoye and Canandaigua Lakes would likely not be as prominent.  Elevation, slope, and the variety of cover types within the landscape may also contribute to the pattern.  Although we cannot explain this as well as we would like, we suggest these as focal areas because others have demonstrated the importance of proximity to water and variety of cover types (Bonter et al. 2009, Nicholls et al. 2001), shown that heterogeneity of slopes and exposures may increase the chances that at least some trees are in bloom and teeming with insects during migration (Wood et al. 2012), and that migrants may stop and refuel at forested sites 45‐60 km from large open water barriers before crossing them (Buler et al. 2007).

Outside of these areas, our data, and other studies, suggest that wooded or shrubby areas with the following characteristics may be valuable somewhat irrespective of their landscape context:

- at least 35% of shrub cover in the understory or shrub cover in nearby areas (see Figures 5 & 6, threshold based on partial plots not shown; Rodewald and Brittingham 2004, Rodewald and Matthews 2005, Suthers et al. 2000)

- multiple species of fruiting shrubs (Figure 6, Appendix G, Buler et al. 2007, Rodewald and Brittingham 2004, Suthers et al. 2000)

- a variety of cover within 1 kilometer (Figure 5, Appendix G, Bonter et al. 2009, Nicholls et al. 2001)

- are quite close to water or a wetland (Appendix G, Bonter et al. 2009, Nicholls et al. 2001).

Indeed, we found moderately high richness and abundance of migrants in patches throughout the study area, and the areas shown in Maps 7 & 8 “capture” approximately 22% of the migrants in the spring and only 7% of the migrants in the fall.  Where woody habitat is abundant on the landscape, migrants use that habitat, although not at the same high densities as they use smaller, more isolated patches near the lake.  While data presented here show that they are not distributed uniformly across the landscape when stopping over, the “hotspots,” or areas of concentrated abundance and/or richness, are not orders of magnitude more “hot” than the rest of the landscape.  Note the range on the maps.  Although our models do under predict the “hotspots” among our own sampling sites, the full range between the “best” sites and “worst” sites for among our sampling sites was only 0.25‐ 9.14 average number of spring migrants per day and 0‐27 average number of fall migrants per day (Table 1).  The “hotspots” may be areas to focus conservation action, particularly in areas where there is little other potential suitable habitat for migrants, but effective conservation of migratory land birds will require a diffuse network of stopover sites, and efforts to improve habitat for migrants by ensuring good shrub cover and diverse food resources is likely valuable _anywhere on the map_ .

When using our maps to identify potential stopover habitat, users should keep in mind the following.

1) These maps do not identify all habitat in the study area that meets the criteria we identified above as important, because current limitations of remotely sensed data prohibited us from mapping some key habitat characteristics, such as the amount of shrub cover or number of fruiting shrubs.

2) As with any remotely sensed land cover dataset, there are errors in the base land cover data that we used.

3) These maps are applicable to land birds only.  Since we limited our sampling to wooded areas, our results are not applicable to grassland birds, wetland birds, shorebirds or waterfowl, and they are likely not applicable to raptors either, since those species migrate during the day and use thermals to travel along and around the lakeshore.

It is also important to point out that habitat used for stopover likely varies considerably in quality, and does not all provide equal value for all migrants.  Although studies suggest that migrants can gain mass in most sites (Seewagen and Slayton 2008), and that isolated patches do not create “traps” such that birds are drawn to sites that result in a cost to fitness, longitudinal studies of reproductive success tied to stopover use are extremely limited, if not completely lacking.  Please see the user guide that accompanies this report and the maps for more information about what can be done to ensure and improve stopover habitat quality for migratory birds, and what to consider if focusing on some of the areas highlighted on these predictive maps.

Only 0.6% of the area identified on Map 7 is currently in some form of protected status, and a much greater percentage of the inland wetland complexes are protected than the shoreline of Lake Ontario.  (Of course, much more of the interior of the study region used to be suitable habitat than currently is, and the Refuges are remnants of the extensive wetland complexes that used to exist).  Examining that statistic in reverse suggests that open space and park planning has either done a good job selecting places important to migratory birds or establishing habitat islands that over time have become some of the only options for migrants in developed or agricultural landscapes‐‐‐more than 50% of the existing protected lands within the study area had some portion that stands out as high value for migrant abundance and richness.  Even in these protected places, there are still threats to migrating birds, however, such as towers around these areas, cats, and toxins accumulating in our waterways and wetlands.  Furthermore, overabundant populations of deer may significantly reduce forest regeneration and some of the important shrub cover in the understory of forests that the migrants are using heavily during both seasons.

These predictions, built from on‐the‐ground data specific to our region, do somewhat validate more coarsely predictive models built from literature review and expert opinion.  Similarities include predicted high values of Great Lakes shorelines, identification of some isolated patches as important, and highlighting inland areas with high variety of cover or proximity to wetlands or other water.  However, the resulting predictions presented here differ in several important ways from both our initial simple model and a Great Lakes region‐wide model that is in draft form (Ewert et al. 2012).  First, the importance of proximity to the Great Lakes extends well beyond the 2km we originally modeled, particularly for the fall, and abundance and richness decline less steeply with increasing distance than new draft region‐wide models predict.  This means that the maps presented here show more habitat as important both within and slightly beyond the coastal zone.  Furthermore, this model predicts important stopover habitat around inland wetland complexes and in the Finger Lakes, far more prominently than our original coarse model, and well beyond the _extent_ of the region‐wide model.  Second, this model predicts that shorelines around embayments are likely to have high concentrations of migrants, at least in the spring‐‐‐our original model did not factor that in, nor has the region‐wide model.  Third, areas of potential habitat isolated in a matrix of mostly developed land cover are predicted to have higher abundance and richness than more intact portions, which is opposite what we hypothesized in our original model.  Although the region‐ wide model does incorporate a similar isolation effect, the maps presented here highlight far more area around Rochester as important than does the region wide map, suggesting perhaps that the threshold used for that model (<15% suitable habitat within a 5 km radius) might be too strict.

Our predictions also somewhat mirror patterns from radar data covering a portion of our study area around Buffalo up to Lake Ontario (Bonter et al. 2009, Bonter personal communication, Buler and Dawson 2012). The important areas in and around the Iroquois‐Tonawanda‐Oak Orchard Wetland Complex also show up as high and consistent use areas based on the fall radar data (Buler and Dawson 2012), as does the band around the

lakeshore inland to approximately 10 km.  There is also concurrence of many of the other areas just east of Buffalo.  The areas on Grand Island, in the Niagara River, however, do not show up as highly or consistently used areas based on the radar data.  Note that these fall radar data from the Buffalo station suggest that the flight patterns in the fall are predominantly to the SW (Buler and Dawson 2012), which may explain the greater importance of areas west of Rochester in the fall, as compared to areas east of Rochester, that we found in our study, as evident on the maps.

Overall, the results of this study, and particularly the maps of predicted migrant use, verify that coastal zones of the Great Lakes are important stopover habitat within New York, as predicted based on other results, and newly suggest that an even wider coastal area is important on southern shores of the Lakes during fall migration.  In our study area, as has been suggested by others, small woodland habitat islands within developed landscapes, and possibly within agricultural landscapes, are also highly utilized.  This is one of the few stopover studies to extend inland beyond the coastal zone, and it shows that at least some inland forest and wetland complexes may be nearly as important stopover habitat as the coastal zones.  The maps presented here should always be used in conjunction with on‐the‐ground assessments of habitat quality, evaluation of threats to existing available habitat, and co‐benefits for other species to prioritize work.  Users should also be aware that remotely sensed data and these models are coarse and that fine‐scale interpretation and use should be done with caution.  We also encourage users to consider these results within the context of the entire Great Lakes region (region‐wide stopover models coming out within the first half of 2013, Ewert et al. 2012) as well as complementary data on NY migration patterns using a different approach (Howard & Schlesinger in prep., Rohrbaugh et al. 2012).  Together, all three of these products should significantly enhance our understanding of land bird migration through the region and increase our ability to effectively conserve it.
